title: Forest type explained about half of the gap between spatial and temporal bird community temperature slopes on 2,523 forested US routes (1966-2025), but not in open-habitat birds, the East, or species
abstract: Question: bird community temperature indices (CTI) of the North American Breeding Bird Survey follow in time only a small part of their spatial temperature slope. Does vegetation, which sorts by climate but changes over centuries, mediate the spatial slope, so that only its vegetation-independent part can appear in decades? Data: BBS 2026 release (1966-2025; 107,922 runs, 466 species, contiguous US), nClimGrid temperature and precipitation, USFS/FIA 250 m forest type maps (28 groups, 133 types). Method: a vegetation thermal index (VTI) per route from the US-wide temperature of each forest type, cross-fitted by 4 degree block; route-mean CTI on temperature with and without VTI and forest share; temporal slopes on route warming trends with route or route x observer fixed effects; 500 joint block-bootstrap resamples; a plan written before the outcomes. Results: on 2,523 forested routes, VTI correlated with temperature at 0.92, and at fixed temperature the CTI increased by 0.21 C per C of VTI (95% CI 0.13-0.28). The total spatial slope was 0.42 (0.40-0.44) C per C; the direct slope was 0.24 (0.18-0.29) with groups and 0.20 (0.14-0.28) with types. Temporal slopes were 0.028 (0.005-0.056) and 0.080 (0.050-0.116). Vegetation removed 47-64% of the gap (pre-registered threshold met only with types). For 157 low-pitched species without observer hearing drift, temporal tracking was 39-63% of the direct slope and vegetation removed 66-82% of the gap. Mediation was strong for forest birds (direct/total 0.40) and absent for open-habitat birds (0.85). It was weak inside the East (0.82; none beyond precipitation and winter temperature), where tracking stayed at 3-21% of the direct slope, and the regional prediction failed. For 394 species, neither the total (-0.18) nor the direct slope (-0.05) predicted the response to differential warming. Conclusion: slow forests explain about half of the continental bird tracking deficit, but not the eastern, local, open-habitat or species-level deficits. Limitations: one vegetation snapshot (about 2004); VTI also carries other climate information; non-forest vegetation not mapped; correlational design.
